output.title: Rollback plans are backup plans, not controls
output.body:
Rollback plans sound sensible until you look at what actually goes wrong in a small business workflow. The issue is usually not, “Can we undo this later?” It is, “What happens while this automation is running?” If the wrong customer reply goes out, a duplicate invoice is created, or a manual step gets skipped, rolling back after the fact does not erase the damage already in motion.

That is why rollback is not enough on its own. It restores the previous state. It does not stop bad data, bad answers, or bad decisions from spreading through the rest of the process. For an owner, the better question is simple: which step needs a gate before anything is committed?

Start with one repeatable workflow you are thinking about automating. Write down the three most damaging failure modes: wrong data, missed items, and duplicates. Then choose one human approval point that would block the worst one before it reaches payment, the inbox, or the CRM. If you are testing invoice extraction, for example, spot-check a few entries against the source documents before anything is posted. That is a control. Rollback is still useful, but it is the backup plan, not the main defense.

Bareni’s policy is to keep customer accounts in the customer’s name and hand over finished code. That is no-lock-in positioning, not a warranty. The practical move is still the same: control the workflow first, then decide whether automation belongs there at all.
